lesson.summary: Understand patterns from first principles, with a small runnable example.

stage.name: Orientation: why design matters
stage.subtitle: Book chapters 1–2
stage.description: Why projects fail, the accidental success of PHP objects, and how the book is organised.

payload.markdown: A pattern describes a problem in software design and provides the kernel of a solution. “Solution” here does not mean the kind of cut-and-paste code that you might find in a cookbook (excellent though cookbooks are as resources for the programmer). Instead, a design pattern describes an approach that can be taken to solve a problem. A sample implementation may be given, but it is less important than the concept that it serves to illustrate. Part 2 begins by defining design patterns and describing their structure. I also look at some of the reasons behind their popularity.

payload.markdown: Patterns tend to promote and follow certain core design principles. An understanding of these can help in analyzing a pattern’s motivation and can usefully be applied to all programming. I discuss some of these principles. I also examine the Unified Modeling Language (UML), a platform-independent way of describing classes and their interactions. Although this book is not a pattern catalog, I examine some of the most famous and useful patterns. I describe the problem that each pattern addresses, analyze the solution, and present an implementation example in PHP.

items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Design Principles: Guidelines such as SOLID that keep object designs flexible.
UML Class & Sequence: Standard diagrams for static structure and runtime interaction.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Behavioral Patterns: Patterns that distribute responsibility and coordinate behaviour.
